title: Find the number of terms needed in a geometric series

say: You give it a geometric series and a target, such as a term that must pass a value. It finds the **number of terms** $n$ needed.
The key idea: $n$ sits in a power, so take logs to bring it down. Then round $n$ to a whole number the right way.

example.question: A geometric sequence has first term $3$ and common ratio $2$. Find the least value of $n$ for which $T_n > 5000$.

steps.title: Write the nth term
steps.say: Write $T_n = ar^{n-1}$ with $a = 3$ and $r = 2$. Then set it greater than $5000$.

steps.title: Isolate the power
steps.say: Divide both sides by $3$, so the power stands on its own.

steps.title: Take logs
steps.say: Take $\ln$ of both sides. The power $\hl{1}{n-1}$ comes down in front. $\ln 2$ is positive, so the inequality keeps its direction when you divide by it.

steps.title: Round up to a whole number
steps.say: $n$ counts terms, so it is a whole number. It must be bigger than $11{\cdot}70$, so the least value is $12$.

title: Write a recurring decimal as a fraction

say: You give it a recurring decimal such as $0.272727\dots$ It gives back the same number as a **fraction**.
The key idea: a recurring decimal is a geometric series. The repeating block is the first term $a$, and shifting along one block multiplies by $r = \frac{1}{10^k}$, so $S_\infty$ gives the fraction.

example.question: Write $0.272727\dots$ as a fraction in its simplest form, using the sum to infinity.

steps.title: Split into a series
steps.say: Write the decimal as a sum of the repeating blocks.

lines.text: Each block is $\frac{1}{100}$ of the one before. It is a geometric series.

steps.title: Find a and r
steps.say: The first block is $\hl{1}{a}$. Each term is $\frac{1}{100}$ times the last, so $\hl{2}{r} = 0.01$.

steps.title: Use the formula
steps.say: $|r| < 1$, so the series has a sum to infinity. Put $\hl{1}{a}$ and $\hl{2}{r}$ into $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.say: Divide top and bottom by $9$.

title: Find values of x for which a geometric series converges

say: You give it a geometric series whose ratio $r$ contains $x$. It finds the interval of $x$ for which the series has a **sum to infinity**.
The key idea: a geometric series converges only when $|r| < 1$. So write $r$ in terms of $x$, then solve that modulus inequality.

example.question: The geometric series $1 + \dfrac{x+1}{3} + \left(\dfrac{x+1}{3}\right)^2 + \cdots$ has a sum to infinity. Find the values of $x$ for which the series converges.

steps.title: Find the ratio
steps.say: The ratio $\hl{1}{r}$ is any term divided by the one before it. Here the first term is $1$, so $\hl{1}{r}$ is the second term.

steps.title: Use the convergence test
steps.say: A geometric series converges only when $|\hl{1}{r}| < 1$. Put the ratio into that test.

lines.text: The test is $|r| < 1$.
This is the boundary. Solve it first, then take the values between.

steps.title: Remove the modulus
steps.say: $|A| < 3$ means $-3 < A < 3$. Multiply the inequality by $3$ so that the modulus is gone.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Subtract $1$ from every part of the inequality.

lines.text: The series converges for $\hl{2}{-4} < x < \hl{2}{2}$. The ends are not included, because $|r| = 1$ does not converge.

title: Derive S∞ as the limit of partial sums

say: You give it the formula for the sum of the first $n$ terms, $S_n$. It finds what $S_n$ settles down to as $n$ grows, which is $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
The key idea: when $|r| < 1$, the power $r^n$ shrinks to $0$. The only part of $S_n$ left is $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.

example.question: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a geometric series is $S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$. Use this to show that $6 + 3 + \dfrac{3}{2} + \cdots$ has a sum to infinity of $12$.

steps.title: Find a and r
steps.say: Read the first term $a$ and the ratio $r$ from the series.

steps.title: Write S_n
steps.say: Put $a = 6$ and $r = \frac{1}{2}$ into the formula for $S_n$.

steps.title: Let n grow
steps.say: As $n$ gets large, $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$ gets closer and closer to $\hl{1}{0}$, because the ratio is smaller than $1$.

lines.text: $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \to \hl{1}{0}$ as $n \to \infty$.

steps.title: Take the limit
steps.say: Replace $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$ by $\hl{1}{0}$. What is left is the sum to infinity.

say: You give it a description of a variable. It says whether the data is **categorical** (nominal or ordinal) or **numerical** (discrete or continuous).
The key idea: ask two questions. Is it a number you can do arithmetic with? If so, can it take any value in a range (continuous) or only separate values like whole numbers (discrete)?

example.question:
A school collects data on its students. Classify each variable as categorical nominal, categorical ordinal, numerical discrete or numerical continuous. How many of the three are numerical?
(i) Shoe size (whole and half sizes)
(ii) Favourite subject
(iii) Time taken to run 100 m

steps.title: Ask: is it a number?
steps.say: First ask if the data is a number you could add or average. If it is, it is **numerical**. If it is a label, it is **categorical**.

lines.text: Shoe size is a number. Time is a number. Favourite subject is a label.

steps.title: Sort the categorical one
steps.say: A label with no natural order is **nominal**. A label with an order, like small, medium, large, is **ordinal**.

lines.text: Favourite subject has no order, so it is categorical nominal.

steps.title: Sort the numerical ones
steps.say: Numerical data is **discrete** if it takes separate values you could list. It is **continuous** if any value in a range is possible.

lines.text: Shoe size: only $\hl{1}{40}$, $\hl{1}{40.5}$, $\hl{1}{41}$, and so on. Separate values, so numerical discrete.
Time: any value like $\hl{1}{12.4}$ or $\hl{1}{12.43}$ seconds is possible, so numerical continuous.

steps.title: Count the numerical ones
steps.say: Shoe size and time are numerical. Favourite subject is not.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{(i) numerical discrete; (ii) categorical nominal; (iii) numerical continuous; } 2 \text{ numerical}

title: Distinguish population and sample; judge generalisation

say: You give it a description of a study. It names the **population** (everyone the question is about), the **sample** (the part actually studied) and says how far the conclusions reach.
The key idea: conclusions only apply to the population the sample was drawn from. A sample from one school cannot speak for all schools.

example.question: A researcher asks 100 students in one Dublin school how many hours they sleep. She wants to know about all 400 000 second-level students in Ireland. Name the population and the sample. Can she use the result for all Irish students? Give a reason.

steps.title: Name the population
steps.say: The **population** is everyone the researcher wants to know about.

lines.text: Population: all second-level students in Ireland.

steps.title: Name the sample
steps.say: The **sample** is the group she actually asked.

lines.text: Sample: the $\hl{1}{100}$ students in the one Dublin school.

steps.title: Judge the reach
steps.say: Ask if the sample is a fair picture of the whole population. One school in one city is not.

lines.text: She asked $\hl{1}{1}$ student in every $4000$, all from one place.

steps.title: State the conclusion
steps.say: Say what the result covers, and give the reason.

lines.text: No. The result only describes students in that school. Students elsewhere may sleep differently, so it should not be applied to all Irish students.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Population: all Irish second-level students. Sample: the 100 students. No, the sample is from one school only.}

title: Find mean, median and mode (incl. frequency tables)

say: You give it a list of numbers, or a **frequency table**. It gives back three ways to say what is typical: the mean, the median and the mode.
The key idea: the mean shares the total out equally, the median is the middle value once the data is in order, and the mode is the value that turns up most.

example.question:
The table shows the number of books 20 students read last month.
Books read, $x$: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Number of students, $f$: 2, 3, 6, 4, 5
Find the mean, the median and the mode.

steps.title: Count the students
steps.say: The frequencies tell you how many values there are. Add them to find $n$.

steps.title: Find the mean
steps.say: Multiply each value by its frequency and add. Then divide by $n$ to get the $\hl{1}{\text{mean}}$.

steps.title: Find the median
steps.say: There are $20$ values, so the $\hl{2}{\text{median}}$ is halfway between the 10th and the 11th. Add the frequencies as you go to find where they sit.

lines.text: Running total: $2, 5, 11, 15, 20$. The 10th and 11th values are both in the group for $x = 3$.

steps.title: Find the mode
steps.say: The $\hl{3}{\text{mode}}$ is the value with the biggest frequency.

lines.text: The biggest frequency is $6$, at $x = 3$.

title: Select a simple random sample and spot bias

say: You give it a population and a way of picking people from it. It tells you whether the sample is a **simple random sample**, and if not, where the bias comes from.
The key idea: in a simple random sample every member has the same chance of being picked. If some people are more likely to be picked, or left out, the sample is biased.

example.question:
A school has 600 students. The principal wants to survey 30 of them about the canteen. She asks the first 30 students who arrive at school in the morning.
Give one reason this sample could be biased. Describe how to pick a simple random sample of 30 instead.

steps.title: Spot the bias
steps.say: Ask who could never be picked. The students who arrive late have no chance, so the sample is not **representative**.

lines.text: Early arrivals may come by school bus or eat breakfast at school. Their views on the canteen may differ from the rest.

steps.title: Number the population
steps.say: A simple random sample needs a full list. Give every student a number from $1$ to $600$.

lines.text: The list is the whole population.

steps.title: Pick at random
steps.say: Use a random number generator or draw numbers from a hat. Pick $30$ different numbers. Those students are the sample.

lines.text: The principal does not choose. Chance decides.

steps.title: Check it is fair
steps.say: Every student must have the same chance of being picked. Work out the chance.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Biased: late arrivals cannot be picked. Fix: number all 600, pick 30 at random, each chance } \frac{1}{20}

title: Identify surveys, observational studies and designed experiments

say: You give it a description of a study. It names the type: a **survey**, an observational study or a designed experiment.
The key idea: ask whether the researcher changed anything. A survey asks questions, an observational study only watches, and an experiment assigns people to different treatments.

example.question:
A researcher wants to know if a new fertiliser makes tomato plants grow taller. She splits 40 plants at random into two equal groups. One group gets the fertiliser and the other does not. After 6 weeks she measures every plant.
What type of study is this? Give a reason.

steps.title: Did she change anything?
steps.say: Ask whether the researcher gave something to the subjects. Here she gave fertiliser to one group only.

lines.text: She applied a treatment. A survey or an observational study never does.

steps.title: Were groups made at random?
steps.say: In an experiment, chance decides who gets the treatment. This keeps the groups alike.

lines.text: Plants were split at random into two groups.

steps.title: Find the group size
steps.say: The groups are equal, so share the plants out evenly.

lines.text: Each group has $20$ plants. One is the treatment group and one is the comparison group.

steps.title: Name the type
steps.say: She applied a treatment to randomly chosen groups and compared the results.

lines.text: This is a **designed experiment**.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Designed experiment: treatment given to random groups of } 20

title: Design a plan and questions to collect data

say: You give it a research question. It gives back a **plan** for collecting the data and survey questions that do not push people toward an answer.
The key idea: every group you care about must get a fair share of the sample, and a question must not hint at the answer you hope for.

example.question: A school of $800$ students has four year groups of $200$. The principal wants to find out what students think of the canteen, and plans to ask: "Don't you agree the canteen food is awful?" She will survey $40$ students. Rewrite the question fairly and say how many students to ask from each year group.

steps.title: Spot the bias
steps.say: A question is **leading** if it hints at the answer. The words "Don't you agree" and "awful" push students toward one reply.

lines.text: The question pushes the student to say yes.

steps.title: Reword it fairly
steps.say: Take out the hint. Ask for an opinion and offer balanced choices.

lines.text: "How would you rate the canteen food?" Very good, good, average, poor, very poor.

steps.title: Find the sampling fraction
steps.say: Each year group should be represented in proportion. $40$ out of $800$ is the fraction of students to ask.

steps.title: Students from each year
steps.say: Each year group has $200$ students. Take that fraction of each, and choose them at random within the year.

lines.text: Ask $10$ students from each of the four year groups.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Ask } 10 \text{ from each year group, using a neutral question}

say: You give it a data set and a percentage. It finds the value that has that percentage of the data **below** it.
The $80$th percentile is the score with $80\%$ of the scores under it, so you find its position by taking that percentage of the number of scores.

example.question:
Twenty students sat a test. Their scores, in order, were:
$34, 41, 45, 48, 52, 55, 57, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70, 71, 73, 75, 78, 82, 85, 91$
Find the $80$th percentile score.

steps.title: Count how many are below
steps.say: The $80$th percentile has $80\%$ of the scores below it. Find $80\%$ of the $20$ scores.

lines.text: So $16$ scores lie below the percentile.

steps.title: Find the cut-off place
steps.say: With $\hl{1}{16}$ scores below, the cut-off is between the $16$th and $17$th scores in the ordered list.

lines.text: $16$th score: $75$
$17$th score: $78$

steps.title: Take the midpoint
steps.say: The cut-off falls exactly between two scores, so take the value halfway between them.

title: Define stratified, cluster and quota sampling; role of randomisation and controls

say: You give it a description of how a study chose its people. It names the method (**stratified**, cluster or quota), and says what bias or control it needs.
The key idea is who gets picked. Stratified splits the group into types and samples each type in proportion. Cluster picks whole groups. Quota fills set numbers but not at random.

example.question: A school has $900$ students: $270$ in 1st year, $225$ in 2nd, $180$ in 3rd, $135$ in 4th and $90$ in 5th. A survey needs a stratified random sample of $60$ students, by year group. Name the method and find how many 3rd years are chosen.

steps.title: Name the method
steps.say: The students are split into year groups and each group is sampled in proportion to its size. That is **stratified** sampling.

lines.text: Each year group is a stratum. Inside each stratum, students must be chosen at random.

steps.title: Find the fraction
steps.say: Each group gets the same fraction of its students. Divide the sample size by the whole school.

steps.title: Apply it to 3rd year
steps.say: Take that fraction of the $180$ third-year students.

lines.text: Choose these $12$ at random from the 3rd years, for example by numbering them and using a random number generator.
